recent_posts.title: Running Google Ads from the terminal with custom AI skills
recent_posts.summary: A growth marketer with 12 years of paid search experience describes how they moved their entire Google Ads operation into Kilo CLI using custom AI skills and Python scripts. The setup includes three core skills: a script library with conventions (dry-run defaults, PAUSED campaign creation, deduplication), a Performance Max search terms audit workflow, and an automated Monday reporting pipeline. Key benefits include model-cost optimization (cheap models for execution, expensive ones for strategy), consistent campaign naming and structure, and a self-improving knowledge base where API quirks discovered mid-task are automatically documented for future sessions. The repo is self-describing via CHANGELOG, todo, and a live campaigns inventory regenerated before each git push.

recent_posts.title: Testing ChatGPT Images 2.0 and GPT-5.5 for landing page generation
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on test of using ChatGPT Images 2.0 and GPT-5.5 to build landing pages via an image-first workflow: generate a design image, iterate on it, then convert to HTML. Three use cases were tested — an AI coding tool page, a SaaS page for lawyers, and a shoe e-commerce site. Results were mixed: modern-style pages translated well, while traditional design styles (e.g., lawyer websites) struggled due to likely gaps in training data. A useful trick emerged: feeding a screenshot back to the model to self-diagnose and fix layout issues. The key takeaway is that AI-assisted design requires a different approach than AI-assisted coding, and more specific prompts are needed for niche design styles.

recent_posts.title: Hermes vs. OpenClaw - When to Reach for Which Agent
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on comparison of two open-source AI agent frameworks — Hermes (from Nous Research, ~135k GitHub stars) and OpenClaw (~369k stars). The core distinction: Hermes is agent-first with a self-improving 'learning loop' and subagent delegation, while OpenClaw is gateway-first with 24+ messaging platform integrations and a 13,700+ community skill ecosystem. Key pitfalls covered include Hermes's flawed self-evaluation and skill overwriting, and OpenClaw's update instability, unreliable memory, and significant security incidents (6 CVEs, 341+ malicious skills). The author runs both in tandem — OpenClaw as orchestrator and Hermes as execution specialist — and provides guidance on model cost management, with daily API costs ranging from $1 to $130+ depending on model choice.

recent_posts.title: Mistral Medium 3.5 is Live in Kilo Code
recent_posts.summary: Mistral Medium 3.5, a 128B dense model merging instruction-following, reasoning, and coding, is now available in Kilo Code. The model scores 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified, supports a 256k context window, ships with open weights under a modified MIT license, and can run self-hosted on as few as four GPUs. It is accessible via the Kilo VS Code extension, CLI, cloud agents, and KiloClaw, priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

recent_posts.title: We're back on Product Hunt — here's how far Kilo has come
recent_posts.summary: Kilo Code is relaunching on Product Hunt after a year of major development. The product has evolved from a simple VS Code AI coding extension to a full agentic development ecosystem. Key new features include an Agent Manager for running multiple parallel agents, git worktree isolation per agent, built-in agent modes (Code, Plan, Debug, Ask), custom subagents, model comparison across 500+ models simultaneously, local code review with line-level comments, and codebase indexing. The platform now spans VS Code, JetBrains, CLI, Cloud Agents, and Slack with a shared engine. The extension has reached 2.3 million installs. The relaunch follows three weeks of intensive community-driven iteration after a major architectural rebuild, including 188 PRs in a single week. Kilo Code remains free and open source.

recent_posts.title: 7 ways AI reduces organizational friction for engineering teams
recent_posts.summary: Enterprise engineering teams often measure AI coding tools by raw code output, but the biggest productivity gains come from reducing organizational friction. Seven underappreciated wins include: converting Slack discussions directly into implementation, enabling non-engineers to submit reviewable PRs via AI agents, accelerating onboarding with codebase-aware Q&A, auto-generating documentation drafts, parallelizing maintenance backlogs, enabling cross-team changes without waiting in backlogs, and enforcing codebase conventions consistently through custom rules. These gains compound across the whole engineering system rather than just speeding up individual developers.

recent_posts.title: KiloClaw in VS Code, Kilo CLI in KiloClaw
recent_posts.summary: Kilo Code shipped two integrations in April: a native KiloClaw chat panel inside the VS Code extension, and the Kilo CLI built into every KiloClaw cloud instance. The VS Code panel (available since v7.2.20) lets developers interact with their always-on autonomous KiloClaw agent alongside their interactive Kilo Code session, using the same WebSocket stream as the web UI. Meanwhile, KiloClaw instances now include the full Kilo CLI, enabling the autonomous agent to spin up coding sessions, review PRs, and coordinate multi-repo changes independently. The /kiloclaw CLI command also gained org-aware support for team contexts. Key limitation: both features require Kilo Gateway authentication.

recent_posts.title: Grok 4.3 Is Live in Kilo Code
recent_posts.summary: Grok 4.3 from xAI is now available in Kilo Code. The model features always-on reasoning (non-configurable), a 1M token context window with no output limit, and competitive pricing at $1.25/$2.50 per million tokens — roughly 5–10x cheaper than comparable reasoning models. It builds on the Grok 4.20 architecture with improved instruction-following, better context retention across long agentic sessions, native video understanding, and structured document generation. xAI estimates a ~20% cost reduction versus 4.20. The model is available immediately in Kilo's IDE, CLI, and cloud agents with no waitlist.

recent_posts.title: Warp Finally Went Open Source
recent_posts.summary: Warp open-sourced its terminal client after five years, but the move comes with caveats: OpenAI is the founding sponsor, the recommended contribution workflow runs through Warp's proprietary Oz platform, AI features still depend on Warp's backend, and BYOK model freedom is locked behind paid plans. Within days, the community forked the project as OpenWarp to enable any OpenAI-compatible endpoint without restrictions. The author contextualizes the timing alongside Roo Code sunsetting and Cursor's acquisition, framing Warp's move as a competitive land grab rather than a purely philosophical shift. The post concludes with a pitch for Kilo as a model-agnostic alternative built with openness from the start.

recent_posts.title: Rebuilding a viral Hacker News game with Kilo CLI + Opus 4.7
recent_posts.summary: A developer rebuilt a viral Hacker News multiplayer cursor game (Cursor Camp) using Kilo CLI with Claude Opus 4.7 in about 2 minutes for ~$3. The build used Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects for real-time cursor state. Key takeaway: when using AI coding agents for complex apps, the bottleneck is choosing the right tech stack, not implementation. Answering the agent's questions upfront and asking 'which stack lets you build this fastest?' leads to better, cheaper results.
